source.title: Features that Make a Difference: Leveraging Gradients for Improved Dictionary Learning
source.authors: Jeffrey Olmo; J. Wilson; Max Forsey; Bryce Hepner; T. Howe; David Wingate

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates SAE-learned latents in GPT-2 models, including their interpretability and effects on model outputs. This is indirect evidence about dictionary features in LLMs, not a test of toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: The study also reports reconstruction-loss, normalized-MSE, dead-latent, feature-similarity, and gradient-direction results. Those evaluate the proposed g-SAE method or related latent properties, but do not directly establish that the model's underlying features are sparse features recoverable by a dictionary, so they are not catalog rows for the tested version.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper proposing gradient-aware TopK SAEs (g-SAEs). It assumes LLM activations are sparse linear combinations of feature directions and uses SAEs as a tool. Its results compare g-SAE against TopK and E2E SAEs on loss added, NMSE, dead latents, steering strength and human-rated interpretability. It reports only its own method's performance relative to other SAEs. No result tests whether features are superposed, whether SAEs recover a model's true features, or whether those features are canonical, complete or one-dimensional. The human-interpretability result is relative across SAE types, and Figure 10's absolute rates are not given in the text.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that g-SAEs explain more of the model's output at a given sparsity and expansion size, and yield latents that steer associated logits more strongly and specifically. They report no measurable cost to human-rated interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a gradient-aware TopK activation rule for SAE dictionary learning, using input-activation gradients when selecting latent activations; it does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering effects are evaluated across layers 3, 5, and 7 and multiple steering scales; the AI example uses layer 5 and α = 100.

fits_no_version.finding: In GPT-2 layers 3+, directions of activation differences have higher directional derivatives of loss than isotropic or covariance-matched random directions. Perturbation norm correlates weakly with change in loss, while the gradient first-order approximation correlates more strongly (Sec. 2.3–2.4, Figs. 2–3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM outputs are especially locally sensitive to perturbations along activation-difference (putative feature) directions compared with random directions.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study does not compare SAE latents with ground-truth model features, so its interpretability and steering results are indirect evidence of feature recovery. The manual evaluation used 3 raters and 384 samples. Numerical scores and uncertainty estimates for several figure-reported comparisons are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Reconstruction and dead-latent comparisons, latent activity densities, and feature-direction similarity results were left out because they evaluate the g-SAE method or its learned-latent properties without directly measuring the version's claim about recovery of the model's underlying sparse features.

untested.parts: No toy models, feature/dimension sweeps, sparsity transition or geometry.
No test of neuron polysemanticity arising from capacity competition; SAE dictionary size is varied only as a method hyperparameter.
No alternative causes of polysemanticity studied.
No measurement of features spread across neurons, and no absolute evidence of SAE feature recovery; only relative comparisons between SAE variants.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not tested. The feature-splitting analysis (decoder cosine similarity) compares SAE types only.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T3/tests classification and its V4 'supports' label are not justified. All four rows compare the proposed g-SAE with other SAE architectures, which is the study's own method compared with others. The paper treats feature sparsity and linearity as premises. Reconstruction, dead-latent and scaling results (Table 1, Figs. 4, 9) are likewise method evaluations and were correctly not catalogued.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-over-dimension sweep, sparsity-dependent transition, or superposition geometry are tested.
The study varies SAE dictionary capacity but does not test whether model neurons become polysemantic through competition for capacity, or whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
No alternative cause of polysemantic neurons is tested.
The study evaluates SAE latents on GPT-2, but does not establish ground-truth feature recovery, measure how features are distributed across neurons, or test other LLM families.
Human interpretability and steering are evaluated, but completeness, stability, and canonical status of SAE features are not.
The study does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features in the underlying model.

rows.subject: human raters
rows.operation_detail: Human raters judged SAE feature interpretability as Yes, Maybe, or No.
rows.value: The authors report that g-SAEs and TopK SAEs were rated similarly interpretable; E2E-TopK SAEs were slightly less interpretable.
rows.note: The text reports the comparison but does not give numerical scores.
rows.check: This compares interpretability across SAE architectures, i.e. the study's own method against others. No absolute monosemanticity rate is given in the text (Figure 10 only), so it cannot show whether SAEs recover interpretable sparse features in GPT-2.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Added decoder-column latent vectors as steering directions and measured probability changes for the logits associated with each latent.

conditions.value: g-SAE compared with TopK and E2E
random samples of latents with L0 = 32
α incremented in steps of 5/3 above and 10 below

rows.measure: Average probability added to the latent's associated logits
rows.value: The authors report that g-SAE associated-logit probability increases were on average over 5x greater than for TopK SAEs.
rows.note: The text gives an aggregate comparison across the plotted settings, not per-layer numerical values.
rows.check: Own-method comparison of steering strength (g-SAE vs TopK). It does not measure whether the model contains sparse features recoverable by a dictionary.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Added decoder-column latent vectors as steering directions and measured probability changes for logits outside each latent's associated set.

conditions.value: g-SAE compared with other SAE types
random samples of latents with L0 = 32
α incremented in steps of 5/3 above and 10 below

rows.measure: Average probability added to logits other than the associated logits
rows.value: The authors report that g-SAE vectors increased the likelihood of arbitrary logits less than the other SAE vectors.
rows.note: The text reports the aggregate direction of the comparison, not per-layer numerical values.
rows.check: Own-method comparison of steering specificity across SAE types. It does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Added steering vectors from the layer-5 latent associated with “AI” and measured changes in probabilities of its top associated logits.
rows.measure: Average probability change for associated logits
rows.value: The authors report that the g-SAE latent steered toward AI-related concepts in a more targeted and potent manner; numerical values are shown only in the figure.
rows.note: The mean probability added to all logits not listed above was 7.3 × 10−1 for g-SAE and 9.0 × 10−1 for TopK, supporting greater targeting for g-SAE.
rows.check: Single-latent example comparing g-SAE with TopK steering, an own-method comparison. Note that 7.3e-1 vs 9.0e-1 are probabilities added to non-listed logits, not to the targeted logits.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GPT-2 small SAE latents in the tested layers and steering settings
reader_labels.reason: The raters judged g-SAE latents similarly interpretable to TopK latents, and g-SAE latent directions produced stronger increases on associated logits with less increase on unrelated logits (r1–r4).
